title: How Browsers Work
summary: A browser is four cooperating engines wearing a UI shell, split across processes for crash isolation and security. This is the mental model everything else in frontend interviews builds on.

slides.markdown:
Ask a frontend candidate "what is a browser" and most describe the address bar. What's actually running is closer to a small **operating system**: several specialized engines, coordinated across multiple OS processes, each one untrusted by design.

That architecture is not trivia — it's the reason a crashed tab doesn't take down your whole browser, why a compromised page can't read your other tabs, and why `defer` vs `async` even matters. Every later topic in this group — rendering, caching, CORS, storage — is a consequence of decisions made at this layer.

This topic builds the map: what a browser *is*, how it's split into processes, and where the engines that parse your HTML, lay out your CSS, and run your JavaScript actually live.

"Browser" is a UI shell wrapped around several distinct engines that don't share responsibilities:

- **The browser engine** — coordinates everything: tabs, navigation, the address bar, bookmarks.
- **The rendering engine** — turns HTML/CSS into pixels (Blink, Gecko, WebKit — more in a later slide).
- **The JavaScript engine** — parses and executes your JS (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore).
- **The networking stack** — handles HTTP, TLS, caching, cookies at the transport level.

They're built and versioned somewhat independently. Chrome's V8 engine, for instance, also powers Node.js and Deno outside any browser at all — proof that "JS engine" and "browser" are genuinely separable concepts, not one monolith.

slides.subTitle: One page, several OS processes
slides.markdown:
A single tab loading a single page typically spans **four or more OS processes**, each with a narrow job:

- **Browser process** — the one "main" process: UI, address bar, disk cache, orchestrates everything else.
- **Renderer process** — parses HTML/CSS, runs your JS, builds the layout. Usually one per site instance.
- **GPU process** — owns the GPU for compositing and rendering acceleration, shared across renderers.
- **Network process** — issues requests, handles the HTTP cache, independent of any one tab.

Open ten tabs and you don't get ten unrelated browsers — you get one browser process, one shared GPU and network process, and roughly ten renderer processes (fewer if site isolation groups some together, more if a page embeds cross-site iframes).

slides.sectionTitle: Why tabs get their own process
slides.subTitle: Crash isolation and site isolation
slides.markdown:
Two separate motivations drive per-tab processes, and interviewers expect you to name both:

- **Crash isolation.** A renderer bug — an infinite loop, a native crash in a media codec — kills only that renderer. You see "Aw, Snap!" on one tab; the rest of the browser, and your other 30 tabs, keep running.
- **Site isolation (security).** Even within a browsing session, `evil.com` and `bank.com` are kept in separate renderer processes so that a memory-safety bug (like a Spectre-style side channel) in one can't read data belonging to the other, because they're never in the same address space.

Site isolation is the stronger of the two claims: it's not just about stability, it's a genuine security boundary that shipped in Chrome specifically as a response to Spectre in 2018.

slides.sectionTitle: Inside the renderer: two threads that matter
slides.subTitle: Main thread vs compositor thread
slides.markdown:
Within one renderer process, two threads do most of the work you can influence from application code:

- **Main thread** — runs your JavaScript, computes style, does layout, and paints. It is single-threaded and one long-running task here blocks everything else on the page, including input handling.
- **Compositor thread** — takes the painted layers and assembles the final frame, and can do this **without** going back to the main thread for certain properties (`transform`, `opacity`).

This split is exactly why `transform`-based animations stay smooth even while the main thread is busy, but animating `width` or `top` does not — the latter forces layout back on the main thread every frame. "Use `transform` for animations" is a direct consequence of this architecture, not an arbitrary best practice.

slides.subTitle: Parse, compile, optimize
slides.markdown:
Inside the renderer, the JS engine runs a pipeline, not a single interpreter step:

1. **Parse** source into an AST.
2. **Compile to bytecode** quickly (an "interpreter tier" — Ignition in V8) so code starts running fast.
3. **Profile while running**, and for "hot" functions called repeatedly with stable argument shapes, **JIT-compile to optimized machine code** (TurboFan in V8).
4. **Deoptimize** back to bytecode if an assumption the optimizer made — like "this argument is always a number" — turns out to be wrong.

That last step explains a real performance gotcha: a function that's fast because it got optimized can silently get slow again if you start calling it with a different shape of object, forcing a deopt.

Renderer processes run **web content you didn't write** — arbitrary HTML, CSS, and JS from any site the user navigates to. Browsers treat them as hostile by default: a renderer runs in an OS-level sandbox with no direct filesystem access, no arbitrary syscalls, and no ability to talk to the network or disk except through narrow, mediated IPC channels to the browser and network processes.

This is why a renderer that gets fully compromised by a malicious page still can't, on its own, read your files or make raw network connections — it has to ask the browser process to do it, and the browser process enforces the rules (same-origin policy, permissions) on that ask. The sandbox is the second wall behind site isolation, not a replacement for it.

slides.subTitle: Same job, different codebases
slides.markdown:
"Browser engine" isn't one thing — three independent codebases implement it, with real behavioral differences:

| Engine | Ships in | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Blink** | Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave | Chromium fork of WebKit (2013); fastest feature-adoption cadence |
| **Gecko** | Firefox | Mozilla's own engine; independent CSS/layout implementation |
| **WebKit** | Safari, all iOS browsers | Apple-controlled; iOS forces every browser to embed it, even "Chrome for iOS" |

The iOS row is the one interviewers probe: Apple's App Store policy requires every browser on iOS — Chrome, Firefox, whatever — to use WebKit under the hood. So "test in three browsers" on iOS still only exercises one rendering engine, and a bug that's WebKit-specific will hit every iOS browser identically.

slides.sectionTitle: The cost of all these processes
slides.markdown:
Multi-process isolation isn't free. Each renderer process carries its own V8 heap, its own copy of shared libraries mapped in, and IPC overhead for every cross-process call — commonly **20–50MB of base overhead per renderer** before a single tab's content is counted.

That's the real reason "Chrome uses too much RAM" is a recurring complaint: 40 tabs isn't 40x one page's memory, it's 40x (page memory + per-process overhead). Browsers mitigate this with tricks like freezing background tabs' renderers and merging same-site renderers under memory pressure — but the trade-off is structural: **stronger isolation always costs more memory**, and every browser is tuning that dial differently.

slides.sectionTitle: One page is not always one process
slides.markdown:
The default mental model — one tab, one renderer process — breaks the moment a page embeds **cross-site content**.

A page from `news.example` embedding an ad iframe from `ads.example` and a payment iframe from `pay.example` can end up as **three separate renderer processes for one visible page**, because site isolation splits by origin, not by tab. Conversely, on memory-constrained devices, the browser may deliberately group multiple same-site frames into one process to save overhead, contradicting the naive "cross-origin always means separate process" assumption too.

Don't reason about "the page's process" — reason about it per-origin. It's the detail that trips up candidates who memorized "one tab = one process" instead of understanding why the split happens.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering "what's the browser doing right now"
slides.markdown:
This question rewards structure over trivia. A strong answer walks outward from process to pixel:

1. **Processes** — one browser process orchestrating a renderer process per site instance, plus shared GPU and network processes.
2. **Inside the renderer** — a main thread running your JS and computing layout, a compositor thread assembling frames.
3. **The engines** — a rendering engine building the DOM/CSSOM, a JS engine parsing and JIT-compiling your code.
4. **The boundary** — every renderer is sandboxed and untrusted, talking to the outside world only through mediated IPC.

Said in that order, in under a minute, it reads as someone who has actually looked under the hood — not someone reciting "the browser renders the page." The rest of this group goes one layer deeper into each piece: the DOM/CSSOM, the render pipeline, and the network layer this architecture sits on top of.
